::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.149", Sentence = "After adjustment for education, ANC and place of delivery, the association weakened and the joint test was no longer significant (p=0.149, 0.159 and 0.182, respectively)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Postnatal care (PNC) is important for maternal and newborn health, but socioeconomic inequalities may limit timely access.
In Malawi, evidence on PNC timing and the pathways linking household wealth to PNC is limited.
We examined socioeconomic inequalities in timely PNC and whether antenatal care (ANC) and delivery-facility type accounted for part of the wealth gradient.
Methodology: We analysed 4,726 women with a live birth in the previous 24 months from the 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Survey.
PNC was timely when the first check occurred within two days of birth, delayed when it occurred later, and absent when no qualifying check was reported.
Survey-weighted multinomial logistic regression examined associations between household wealth and PNC timing, with sequential adjustment for maternal education, ANC and place of delivery.
The slope index of inequality (SII) and relative index of inequality (RII) summarised inequality.
Pathway analyses examined ANC and delivery-facility type as mediators.
Results: Overall, 66.6% of women received timely PNC, 5.1% delayed PNC and 28.3% no PNC.
Unadjusted, women in the richer and richest wealth quintiles had lower relative risk ratios (RRR) of no PNC than women in the poorest quintile (RRR 0.56 and 0.57, respectively).
After full adjustment, the richer group remained less likely to have no PNC (RRR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50-0.89).
Wealth inequality persisted (SII -8.4 percentage points, 95% CI -14.8 to -2.0; RII 0.74, 95% CI 0.59-0.93).
Among all births, 26.6% of the wealth association with no PNC was accounted for by ANC and place of delivery, primarily home delivery.
Conclusion: Timely PNC remains unequally distributed by household wealth in Malawi.
The findings suggest that reducing missed PNC opportunities requires attention to socioeconomic barriers and continuity from pregnancy through delivery and the postnatal period.

Postnatal care (PNC), a crucial part of the maternal and newborn health continuum, remains largely overlooked despite the high concentration of preventable maternal and neonatal deaths occurring in the period immediately following childbirth(1-3) .

The first six weeks after birth offer a critical window to identify and manage complications, and to provide essential counseling and support on breastfeeding, family planning, and newborn care (4) (5) (6).

text.text: However, health systems typically prioritize antenatal and intrapartum care, allocating fewer resources and less attention to postnatal services.
This imbalance is also reflected in the limited research available on PNC (4).
Evidence from low-and middleincome countries consistently reveals that contact with maternity services during pregnancy and childbirth often fails to translate into timely postnatal care.
For instance, in Bangladesh, PNC from a medically trained provider within two days increased from 16% in 2004 to 52% in 2017 (7).

text.text: Yet, significant disparities persisted, with women from the poorest households, those delivering at home, and those who received no antenatal care (ANC) being the least likely to receive PNC (7, 8).
text.formatted: Yet, significant disparities persisted, with women from the poorest households, those delivering at home, and those who received no antenatal care (ANC) being the least likely to receive PNC <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">8)</ref>.

text.text: A pooled analysis of 23 countries similarly found that only 41.4% of women received quality maternal PNC, with higher ANC attendance and facility delivery correlating with increased use (9).

text.text: Ethiopia reinforces this trend: only 16.5% of women received PNC within two days (10).

text.text: Women with at least four ANC visits had substantially higher odds of timely PNC (aOR 2.50, 95% CI 1.42-4.42), and institutional delivery was strongly associated with timely care (aOR 14.55, 95% CI 2.21-95.77) (10) .

text.text: In rural Tanzania, only 14.6% of women sought PNC within 48 hours (11).
text.formatted: In rural Tanzania, only 14.6% of women sought PNC within 48 hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative data pointed to limited knowledge, inadequate provider scheduling, workload, and service constraints as additional barriers to postnatal care (11).
text.formatted: Qualitative data pointed to limited knowledge, inadequate provider scheduling, workload, and service constraints as additional barriers to postnatal care <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these studies indicate an incomplete transition from ANC and delivery to PNC, highlighting the relevance of both socioeconomic status and prior engagement with maternal health services in determining whether women receive timely care.
However, the precise relationship between these factors is less clear.

While evidence consistently links wealth to PNC use (1,12), and ANC and facility delivery to subsequent postnatal contact (6, 10), these factors may represent interconnected stages rather than independent determinants.

For instance (16) reported that 48.4% of women received skilled PNC within 42 days in the 2015-16 MDHS, while (17) found that only 3% of rural women received maternal PNC within 24 hours.

text.text: Although these studies employ different measures and timeframes, they consistently point to persistent gaps in postnatal contact, especially among women who do not deliver in health facilities.
Despite this evidence, the socioeconomic pattern in timely PNC in Malawi has not been examined as a sequence of connected stages of care.

Previous studies have identified ANC attendance, residence, employment, mode of delivery and delivery-facility type as correlates of PNC use (16, 19, 20), but they have generally treated PNC as a binary outcome or used a single timing threshold.

text.text: It therefore remains unclear whether household wealth distinguishes women who receive PNC on time from those who receive it late or not at all, and to what extent differences in ANC attendance and place of delivery account for this pattern.
It is also important to establish whether the wealth gradient persists among women who have already delivered in a health facility.

This study examines socioeconomic inequalities in the timing of PNC in Malawi, distinguishing timely, delayed and absent care, and assesses the extent to which ANC attendance and delivery-facility type account for the observed wealth differences.
We did a cross-sectional analysis of the 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Survey (MDHS), a nationally representative household survey.
The survey was implemented by the National Statistical Office with technical assistance from ICF through The DHS Program.
Fieldwork took place from 13 May to 31 August 2024.
The survey used a stratified two-stage cluster design, selecting 792 clusters and about 23,760 households.
We used the Women's Individual Recode file, which holds the birth history and the maternal and newborn care modules.
Eligible women were aged 15-49 years and had a live birth in the 24 months before interview.
For women with more than one such birth, we analysed the most recent.
We excluded records with a zero sampling weight, which removes the Dzaleka refugee-camp domain that the MDHS reports separately.
We then excluded women with missing data on any model variable (n=27) and women who reported a check by a qualified provider but whose timing was unknown or missing (n=88).
The analytic sample comprised 4,726 women, of whom 4,593 delivered in a health facility ( S1 Table).

text.text: All participants were women by design, so we did not analyse by sex or gender.
We used anonymised, publicly available secondary data from The DHS Program, which were accessed for research purposes on 20 September 2026.
The authors had no access to information that could identify individual participants during or after data collection.
Ethical approval and informed consent for the survey were obtained by the survey implementers, so no further ethical approval was required for this analysis.
We followed the STROBE guideline for cross-sectional studies.
The outcome was the timing of the first postnatal check, in three mutually exclusive categories.
A check counted if it was done by a doctor, clinical officer or medical assistant, a nurse or midwife, or a patient attendant.
Checks by other providers, including traditional birth attendants and community health workers, were treated as no check.
We took the earlier of the check before discharge from the facility and the check after discharge or after a home delivery as the first check, and converted its timing to hours since delivery.
Timely PNC was a first check during the first two days after birth (reported at under 72 hours, or at two days or less, following the DHS definition).
Delayed PNC was a first check later than this, including after 41 days.
No PNC was no qualifying check at any time.
We separated delayed from no PNC because they reflect different failures of care: contact that comes too late, and contact that never happens.
The main explanatory variable was household wealth, measured by the DHS wealth quintile (poorest to richest).
Maternal education was categorised as none, primary, secondary or higher.
ANC use was the number of visits for the most recent birth (none, 1-3, or four or more).
Delivery-facility type had four categories: public, CHAM or mission, private (NGO and non-NGO), and other and home delivery.
In analyses of facility births, we used the first three categories.

All models adjusted for maternal age at birth (under 20, 20-34, 35-49 years), birth order (1, 2-3, 4-5, 6 or more), marital status (married or living with a partner; formerly married, which includes widowed, divorced and separated; never married), urban or rural residence, and region (Northern, Central, Southern).
Caesarean delivery was described but not used in the models, because it follows the choice of facility and may lie on the pathway.
All analyses accounted for the complex survey design.

text.text: Together, these perspectives suggest that socioeconomic position shapes access to maternal health services and that contact with ANC and delivery services may influence subsequent PNC.
Household wealth is the main exposure and may influence timely PNC through ANC utilization, delivery-facility type and direct socioeconomic constraints.
Wealthier women may have greater ability to attend ANC, access different types of delivery facilities and meet the costs associated with seeking care.

ANC may provide information about postnatal care and establish contact with health services before delivery, while delivery-facility type may influence the opportunity to receive a postnatal check before discharge.
Wealth may also remain associated with PNC timing after accounting for these factors through transport costs, competing demands and other barriers to care.

Maternal education is considered an additional resource that may account for part of the wealth gradient, while age, birth order, marital status, residence and region are treated as demographic and contextual characteristics.

The framework distinguishes timely PNC, delayed PNC and no PNC because these outcomes represent different points of failure in the care pathway.
Delayed PNC indicates that contact occurred but not within the recommended period, whereas no PNC indicates that postnatal care was not initiated.
The analysis therefore examines whether the wealth gradient differs across these outcomes and whether it is attenuated after accounting for ANC utilization and delivery-facility type.
Among women who delivered in a health facility, the analysis further assesses whether socioeconomic inequalities in timely PNC persist.
Because the data are cross-sectional and wealth is measured at the time of interview, the framework represents a conceptual ordering rather than a causal model.

The pathway follows the temporal sequence of ANC, delivery and PNC and provides the basis for examining whether differences in ANC utilization and delivery-facility type are associated with the observed wealth gradient in PNC timing.

This study identified four main findings.

First, although two-thirds of women received postnatal care within two days of childbirth, more than one-quarter received no postnatal care, indicating that substantial gaps remain despite the high level of facility delivery in Malawi.
Second, postnatal care showed a clear socioeconomic gradient, with poorer women less likely to receive timely care and more likely to receive no care.
Third, the wealth gradient was partly explained by maternal education, antenatal care and place of delivery, but remained after adjustment.

Finally, home delivery accounted for a significant part of the wealth-related inequality in postnatal care, whereas antenatal care and type of facility among women who delivered in a facility explained little of the remaining inequality.
The proportion receiving timely postnatal care in Malawi was higher than that reported in several previous studies, although differences in definitions and timing criteria limit direct comparisons.

For example (10), reported that only 16.5% of women in Ethiopia received postnatal care within two days, while (7) found that 52% of women in Bangladesh received postnatal care from a medically trained provider within two days in 2017. (6) also reported that only 41.4% of women received quality maternal postnatal care across 23 lowand middle-income countries.

text.text: The relatively higher coverage observed in Malawi may partly reflect the high proportion of institutional births, which creates an opportunity for mothers and newborns to come into contact with health workers immediately after delivery.
However, the finding that 28.3% received no postnatal care shows that contact with maternal health services before or during childbirth does not necessarily translate into postnatal follow-up.
Socioeconomic inequality was particularly evident in the difference between receiving timely care and receiving no care.
Women in the poorest households had the highest prevalence of non-use, while women in richer households were more likely to receive timely care.
Similar socioeconomic gradients have been reported in Bangladesh by (7), in Ethiopia by (25), and in India by (26).

text.text: In the present study, however, wealth was not clearly associated with delayed postnatal care.

This suggests that socioeconomic disadvantage may be more important in determining whether women receive postnatal care at all than in determining whether care is delayed once contact has been established.

Financial constraints, transport costs, competing household responsibilities and the resources required to return to a health facility may make it particularly difficult for poorer women to initiate postnatal care after childbirth.
Maternal education and antenatal care were also strongly related to postnatal care.

Women with higher education and those who attended ANC more frequently were more likely to receive timely postnatal care. (26) similarly reported positive associations between maternal education, household wealth and postnatal care in India, while (7) identified lack of ANC as an important characteristic among women who did not receive postnatal care in Bangladesh.

text.text: Education may improve knowledge of maternal and newborn danger signs, understanding of the importance of postnatal checks and confidence in navigating health services.
Antenatal care provides repeated opportunities to communicate this information and prepare women for care after delivery.
However, the pathway analysis in this study showed that ANC alone did not significantly account for the wealth gradient.
This suggests that having more ANC contacts does not necessarily ensure continuity into the postnatal period.

The content of counselling, preparation for postnatal follow-up and the extent to which women are actively linked to services after delivery may be more important than the number of ANC contacts alone.
Place of delivery provided a clearer explanation of the socioeconomic difference.
Women who delivered at home were substantially less likely to receive timely postnatal care and were much more likely to receive no care than women who delivered in health facilities.

Home delivery also represented the only statistically significant pathway through which . wealth accounted for part of the difference in postnatal care, explaining approximately 27% of the total association with non-use. (16, 27, 28) similarly identified home delivery as an important barrier to timely postnatal care in Bangladesh.

text.text: The explanation is plausible because facility delivery creates an immediate opportunity for maternal and newborn assessment, counselling and initiation of postnatal care before discharge, whereas women delivering at home must make a separate decision to seek care after childbirth.
This additional step may be particularly difficult for women with fewer economic resources.
Importantly, however, the analysis restricted to facility births showed that socioeconomic inequality did not disappear.
Among women who delivered in a health facility, the indirect pathway through facility type explained only a small and statistically non-significant proportion of the wealth gradient.
This finding suggests that increasing institutional delivery, although important, may not be sufficient to eliminate socioeconomic differences in postnatal care.
A similar pattern was reported by (26) in India, where socioeconomic differences in postnatal care persisted despite high levels of institutional delivery.

text.text: Evidence from rural Malawi also provides a useful explanation.

Kim et al. found that the availability of health facilities did not consistently translate into greater use of maternal and newborn postnatal care, suggesting that physical access alone does not guarantee utilisation.

Differences in counselling, discharge practices, awareness of the need for follow-up, provider responsiveness and the ability to return to the facility may therefore become more important once women have overcome the initial barrier of reaching a facility.
The persistence of inequality after adjustment was also evident in the SII and RII estimates.
Although adjustment for education, ANC and place of delivery reduced the magnitude of socioeconomic inequality, a significant gradient remained.
This indicates that the observed differences were not confined to the poorest and richest households but extended across the socioeconomic distribution.

Regional differences in postnatal care further suggest that household resources operate within a wider health-system and geographic context. (29) reported substantial geographic variation in the quality of newborn postnatal care in Ethiopia, while (26) found marked regional differences in postnatal care in India.

The use of secondary data also limited the analysis to variables collected in the MDHS.

Important factors that may influence postnatal care, including the quality and content of counselling, discharge practices, provider behaviour, continuity of care and women's experiences at health facilities, were not adequately captured.
Information on ANC, place of delivery and timing of postnatal care was based on maternal report and may therefore be affected by recall or reporting error.
Residual confounding is also possible despite adjustment for available sociodemographic and maternal characteristics.

Survey allowed the analysis to examine socioeconomic inequalities in postnatal care at the population level.
The study also combined multivariable regression with absolute and relative measures of inequality and pathway analysis, allowing the wealth gradient to be examined from different perspectives.

The analysis further assessed whether the inequality persisted among women who delivered in a health facility, providing a useful comparison of the pathways operating before and after facility delivery.

A key limitation was the cross-sectional nature of the data, which prevented us from establishing temporal or causal relationships between socioeconomic position, antenatal care, place of delivery and postnatal care.

The strong association between home delivery and non-use of postnatal care, together with the significant pathway through home delivery, supports continued efforts to reduce home births and to strengthen mechanisms linking women who deliver outside health facilities to postnatal services.

However, the persistence of socioeconomic inequality among women who delivered in a facility suggests that institutional delivery alone is unlikely to remove the gap.ANC and delivery care therefore provide important opportunities to prepare women for postnatal follow-up.
Counselling should clearly communicate the timing and importance of postnatal care, while discharge procedures could include active referral or scheduling of follow-up where feasible.
Community health workers may also have an important role in identifying mothers and newborns who do not receive timely care, particularly among poorer and rural households.

Because education, ANC and place of delivery accounted for only part of the wealth gradient, efforts should also address barriers that arise after facility delivery, including the ability to return for follow-up and continuity between facility and community services.
Monitoring postnatal care by socioeconomic position and region will be important to ensure that improvements in overall coverage do not conceal persistent inequalities.
